stories.body: The United States is considering an indefinite naval blockade of Iran as negotiations over the Strait of Hormuz remain stalled. Vice President JD Vance said Washington’s aims were to stabilise US energy prices, prevent Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons and emerge from the conflict in a position of strength. Iran says it still controls the strait and will not reopen it until its demands over US aggression, reparations and sanctions are met, while shipping traffic has fallen sharply and both sides have imposed restrictions on maritime movement.
stories.headline: US considers an indefinite naval blockade of Iran amid deadlocked talks

stories.body: The United Arab Emirates accused Iran of attacking two vessels linked to state oil company ADNOC while they transited the Strait of Hormuz, calling the incident piracy and a threat to global energy security; no injuries were reported. Separately, salvage crews are moving to stabilise the leaking tanker Caroline Bezengi off Oman, where oil has reached the coast and satellite analysis suggests the slick has expanded to about 1,300 square kilometres. A separate spill linked by analysts to a strike on the Minoan Pioneer has washed up on Iran’s Qeshm Island, threatening mangroves, coral habitats, turtle nesting sites and fishing communities.
stories.headline: UAE accuses Iran of attacking two ADNOC vessels in the Strait of Hormuz as oil spill response begins off Oman

stories.body: At least four people have died in eastern Japan after record rainfall struck Chiba prefecture near Tokyo, causing flooding, landslide warnings, power cuts and transport disruption. Authorities issued their highest emergency warning, evacuated or advised more than 400,000 people to leave at-risk areas, and said rainfall reached roughly 115mm an hour in places. Nearly 7,000 travellers spent the night at Tokyo’s Narita airport, while rescue operations continued amid warnings that flooded rivers and landslide risks remained dangerous.
stories.headline: Japan's unprecedented rains kill four and strand thousands at an airport

stories.body: Romania has shut down the second and final operating reactor at its Cernavodă nuclear plant after prolonged heat and drought pushed the Danube to extremely low levels, limiting water needed for cooling. The plant’s two reactors normally provide about one-fifth of Romania’s electricity, and operators do not expect a restart for at least 10 days. The shutdown has prompted an energy emergency, greater reliance on fossil-fuel generation and imports, and concern in neighbouring Moldova, which depends heavily on Romanian electricity to cover its own shortages.
stories.headline: Romania shuts its only nuclear plant as drought drives the Danube to a record low

stories.body: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has reached a sixth province after a man who travelled from Haut-Uele died in Bas-Uele. More than 2,100 people have died among over 4,500 recorded cases, according to government figures, making the Bundibugyo-strain outbreak the fastest-moving on record. Researchers say genetic evidence points to a new animal-to-human spillover event rather than re-emergence from an earlier outbreak, but the virus is now spreading predominantly between people; there is no approved vaccine or treatment for this strain.
stories.headline: Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo spreads to a sixth province

stories.body: US lawmakers are demanding answers about reported conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, whose deployment has extended beyond 250 days at sea after it was sent to the Middle East during the Iran war. Families and military publications have reported shortages of supplies and fresh food, plumbing and water problems, disrupted mail, exhaustion and deteriorating mental health, including allegations that sailors attempted to jump overboard. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the reports were misrepresented, while senators have called for an investigation and a congressional visit to the carrier.
stories.headline: Conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln raise alarms after more than 250 days at sea

stories.body: White House border czar Tom Homan defended Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s plan to buy thousands of electric shock gloves, saying they could give officers a less-lethal means to gain compliance and avoid deadly force. ICE is considering spending up to $20m on the devices, which deliver a painful electric shock on contact with bare skin. Civil-rights groups, congressional Democrats and some use-of-force experts have criticised the proposal amid wider concerns about immigration enforcement tactics, while officials say training and policy details are still being developed.
stories.headline: Federal officials defend proposed electric shock gloves for immigration officers

stories.body: Flock Safety has announced changes to its nationwide network of automated licence-plate readers following criticism from civil-liberties advocates, lawmakers and communities concerned about mass surveillance and misuse. By January, law-enforcement customers will be required to use auditing systems intended to detect abnormal searches, link searches to a specific case through records-management codes, and accept automatic review of emergency overrides. The company will also cut its standard data-retention period from 30 days to seven, though records connected to cases may be retained longer.
stories.headline: Flock changes its license-plate reader network amid surveillance backlash

stories.body: A new report forecasts that US colleges and universities will enrol about 111,000 fewer international students following a visa crackdown, a decline of nearly 10 percent. The projected reduction could affect institutions that rely on foreign-student enrolment and tuition revenue, as tighter immigration and visa policies reshape the outlook for incoming students.
stories.headline: Report forecasts roughly 110,000 fewer international students at US colleges after visa crackdown

stories.body: The Trump administration says Medicaid will stop covering gender-affirming surgeries and hormone treatment for transgender minors, while the Children’s Health Insurance Program will not cover such treatment for people under 19. The policy would continue mental-health coverage and phase out hormone-treatment coverage for those already receiving it by April 2027. LGBTQ+ advocates said the move would be challenged in court, while the administration described the restrictions as protecting children; many major medical organisations support access to gender-affirming care.
stories.headline: Medicaid says it will stop covering some gender-affirming care for transgender minors

stories.body: Spain has increased police and Civil Guard deployments in Ceuta and is seeking to accelerate the removal of migrants following mass arrivals at the North African enclave in late July. Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said about 5,000 migrants remain in the city, while local authorities estimate a higher total, and said additional officers would process international-protection cases and removals more quickly. Morocco has also reinforced its side of the border ahead of online calls for another mass crossing, while Spanish officials warn migrants not to follow traffickers’ promises.
stories.headline: Spain accelerates expulsions after the mass arrival of migrants in Ceuta

stories.body: Wildfires in Huelva and Huesca have worsened after fresh flare-ups, forcing further evacuations and threatening homes and cultural sites. The Niebla fire in Huelva, which has been burning for a week, has reportedly burned more than 31,000 hectares, making it the largest recorded wildfire in Andalusia, with hundreds of people kept away from affected areas. In Huesca, a renewed fire front near Las Peñas de Riglos prompted evacuations in four more communities, while firefighters worked to protect the old and new monasteries of San Juan de la Peña.
stories.headline: Wildfires in Huelva and Huesca worsen as new flare-ups force evacuations

stories.body: Spain has weather warnings in place across every region except Asturias, with 11 autonomous communities at orange alert for severe heat, heavy rain or thunderstorms. Temperatures are expected to reach 40C in parts of Andalusia, Aragon, Castilla-La Mancha and Catalonia, while some areas also face hail, strong winds and intense rainfall. The alerts come as extreme heat continues across much of Europe, where France has endured a prolonged heatwave and wildfires have triggered evacuations in Greece.
stories.headline: Spain faces extreme heat, rain and storm alerts across nearly the entire country

stories.body: Catalonia’s government has confirmed four new cases of African swine fever in wild boar, including two in Barcelona and one each in Molins de Rei and Esplugues de Llobregat, bringing the outbreak total to 379 positive animals. More than 11,000 wild boar have been tested since the outbreak began near Collserola nine months ago. Nineteen municipalities, including Barcelona, remain in the high-risk zone, and authorities do not expect to ease restrictions in the immediate future despite describing recent capture and infection data as encouraging.
stories.headline: Barcelona records new African swine fever cases as restrictions continue around Collserola

stories.body: Barcelona is expected to see a final surge of extreme heat, with temperatures exceeding 35C widely and potentially reaching 38C or 39C in higher parts of the city, while overnight lows in the centre may remain near 29C. From the weekend, cooler upper-level air is expected to bring more seasonable temperatures and an increasing chance of showers and thunderstorms. Catalonia has already recorded a historic 17 days this year with temperatures above 40C somewhere in the region, while Barcelona has also registered record numbers of torrid nights.
stories.headline: Extreme heat peaks in Barcelona before cooler, more unsettled weather arrives

stories.body: Catalonia’s health system recorded nearly 450 eye-related emergency visits over two days coinciding with the total solar eclipse, including 239 hospital visits and 165 visits to primary-care centres on the day of the event. Emergency services received more than 140 eclipse-related calls and treated dozens of people for eye symptoms such as blurred vision, dryness and irritation. Health officials warn that retinal injuries from viewing an eclipse without proper protection may not become apparent for days or even weeks.
stories.headline: Nearly 450 eye-related emergency visits were reported in Catalunya after the solar eclipse
